chunks.text: The UK government has announced a ban on social media for under-16s. The apps named so far are Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and X.
Australia has gone further: its list also includes Kick, Reddit, Threads and Twitch.
Messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Signal are not expected to be included, and gaming sites such as Roblox sit in an unclear middle.
The details matter, because a ban needs an exemption list and a way to check ages.

The government says it will use “highly effective age assurance”, a term that covers facial age estimation, photo ID matching and digital identity services. The regulator, Ofcom, will be expected to enforce it.
Not everyone is comfortable. YouTube said it was “a vital resource for young people” and argued that a ban risked pushing children towards “anonymous, less safe services”.
Ofcom told the government that checks at 16 are harder than checks at 18, because there is less identity data to compare.
Roblox said it had already expanded its own tools to estimate a user’s age.
Then there is the question of bypassing. A VPN can disguise a user’s location, and some children already use one.
The children’s minister said there were “options” for age-gating VPN use.
The prime minister said it was inevitable that some teenagers would try to get around the rules, but that this did not mean the legislation was wrong.
The timetable is tight. The government said it wanted a vote by the end of 2026 and the rules in force early in 2027.
A professor of internet law warned that secondary legislation can be challenged in the courts, which could delay it.
Meanwhile, Australia’s early results are not encouraging: one survey found that 61% of 12–15-year-olds who had used restricted platforms still had access to at least one account.
Read the verbs and you can hear the argument. A company says; a regulator tells; a professor warns; a minister claims.
